**Why JavaFX? Real-World Applications** 

Before we start coding, understand where JavaFX is used in the real world: 

| Real-World System  | How JavaFX Is Used |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Automotive   Dashboards** | Modern, hardware-accelerated UI for car infotainment systems (e.g.,  digital speedometers and media centers) |
| **Medical Devices**  | Highly visual interfaces for MRI, ultrasound, and patient monitors |
| **Enterprise Trading  Desks** | High-performance charts and real-time data visualization |
| **IoT Control Panels**  | Rich dashboards for managing smart homes and factories |
| **SaaS Dashboards** | Web-like desktop applications (e.g., AWS, Stripe) built with modern UI  standards |

**Why learn JavaFX?** 

1\. **It's the future of Java GUIs** — JavaFX is actively developed and supports hardware  acceleration (GPU). 

2\. **CSS Styling** — You can style JavaFX applications using CSS, just like websites\!

Page **2** of **22**   
3\. **FXML & Scene Builder** — Allows you to build UIs visually and keep design separate from  logic. 

**Setup: Prepare Your Environment in NetBeans** 

NetBeans makes JavaFX setup incredibly easy. Let's get started. 

**Step 0.1: Install Scene Builder** 

1\. Go to **https\://gluonhq.com/products/scene-builder/** 

2\. Download the installer for your OS. 

3\. Run the installer and complete the setup. 

**Step 0.2: Link Scene Builder to NetBeans** 

1\. Open **NetBeans**. 

2\. Go to **Tools → Options** (Windows) or **NetBeans → Preferences** (Mac). 3\. Click on **Java** → **JavaFX**. 

4\. Under **Scene Builder Home**, click **Browse** and select the folder where Scene Builder was  installed (e.g., C:\\Program Files\\Scene Builder). 

5\. Click **OK**.

package programmaticdemo; 

import javafx.application.Application; 

import javafx.scene.Scene; 

import javafx.scene.control.Button; 

import javafx.scene.control.Label; 

import javafx.scene.layout.VBox; 

import javafx.stage.Stage; 

public class Main extends Application { 

 @Override 

 public void start(Stage primaryStage) { 


 *// 1\. Create Nodes (Components)* 

 Label titleLabel \= new Label("My First JavaFX App");

Page **5** of **22**   
 Button clickButton \= new Button("Click Me\!"); 

 *// Add an action to the button* 

 clickButton.setOnAction(e \-\> { 

 titleLabel.setText("Button was clicked\!"); 

 System.out.println("Button clicked on: " \+ Thread.currentThread().getName());  }); 

 *// 2\. Create a Layout Pane and add Nodes to it* 

 VBox root \= new VBox(15); *// 15 is the spacing between elements*  root.getChildren().addAll(titleLabel, clickButton); 


 *// Center the elements and add styling* 

 root.setStyle("-fx-alignment: center; \-fx-padding: 20px; \-fx-background-color: \#f0f0f0;"); 

 *// 3\. Create a Scene and attach the root layout* 

 Scene scene \= new Scene(root, 400, 300); 

 *// 4\. Set the Scene on the Stage (Window)* 

 primaryStage.setTitle("JavaFX Programmatic App"); 

 primaryStage.setScene(scene); 


 *// 5\. Show the Window* 

 primaryStage.show(); 

 }

**Step 1.4: Run the Application** 

1\. Right-click anywhere inside the Main.java file. 

2\. Select **Run File** (or press Shift \+ F6). 

**Expected Output** 

A window will pop up with a label "My First JavaFX App" and a "Click Me\!" button. Click the button. The label text changes, and the terminal prints: 

Button clicked on: JavaFX Application Thread 

*(Notice the thread name\! This is the JavaFX equivalent of the Swing EDT. All UI updates must  happen on this thread.)* 

**Step 1.5: Self-Check Questions** 

**Q1: What is the difference between a Stage and a Scene?** 

\`Stage\` is the physical window (with the title bar). \`Scene\` is the content inside the window. A  Stage can only show one Scene at a time, but you can swap Scenes.  

**Q2: What is the name of the JavaFX main thread?** 

\`JavaFX Application Thread\`. Just like the EDT in Swing, all UI updates must be done on this  thread.

Professional apps need pixel-perfect organization. JavaFX layout panes are more powerful than  Swing's layout managers because they support automatic resizing, spacing, and alignment out  of the box.

**Activity 3: Scene Builder and FXML** 

**Purpose** 

Learn to design JavaFX UIs visually using Scene Builder, separating the UI design from the Java  logic. 

**Learning Outcome addressed:** \#2, \#4 

**Time:** 60 minutes 

 **Real-World Application** 

In enterprise teams, UI designers use Scene Builder to create the layout, while Java developers  write the logic. FXML is the bridge that connects them. This workflow is used by companies like  Gluon, Oracle, and thousands of others. 

**Step 3.1: Create the FXML File** 

1\. Right-click the programmaticdemo package → **New → Empty FXML...** 2\. Name it login. 

3\. Click **Next**. 

4\. Select **Use JavaFX Scene Builder**. 

5\. Click **Finish**. 

*(If NetBeans doesn't open Scene Builder automatically, right-click* login.fxml *in the Projects panel  and select **Open**).* 

**Step 3.2: Design in Scene Builder**

Page **11** of **22**   
1\. You will see a blank canvas. 

2\. Drag a **VBox** from the Library panel (left) onto the canvas. (This is your root container). 3\. In the **Properties** panel (right), set: 

o **Spacing:** 15 

o **Alignment:** CENTER 

o **Padding:** 20 (top, right, bottom, left) 

4\. Drag a **Label** into the VBox. Set **Text:** Login. 

5\. Drag a **TextField** into the VBox. Set **Prompt Text:** Username and **fx:id:** usernameField. 

6\. Drag a **PasswordField** into the VBox. Set **Prompt Text:** Password and **fx:id:** passwordField. 

7\. Drag a **Button** into the VBox. Set **Text:** Login and **fx:id:** loginButton. 

8\. Save (Ctrl \+ S) and close Scene Builder.

**Activity 4: Wiring FXML with a Controller** 

**Purpose** 

Connect the visual FXML file to Java code to make the UI interactive. 

**Learning Outcome addressed:** \#4 

**Time:** 45 minutes 

 **Real-World Application** 

MVC (Model-View-Controller) is the standard architecture for enterprise applications. The FXML  is the View, and the Controller is where all the button clicks and data validation happen. 

**Step 4.1: Create the Controller Class** 

1\. Right-click the programmaticdemo package → **New → Java Class**. 

2\. Name it LoginController. 

3\. Paste this code: 

java 

package programmaticdemo; 

import javafx.fxml.FXML; 

import javafx.scene.control.Button; 

import javafx.scene.control.PasswordField;

Page **13** of **22**   
import javafx.scene.control.TextField; 

public class LoginController { 

 *// The @FXML annotation injects the UI component from the FXML file*  @FXML private TextField usernameField; 

 @FXML private PasswordField passwordField; 

 @FXML private Button loginButton; 

 @FXML 

 private void handleLoginButtonAction() { 

 String username \= usernameField.getText(); 

 String password \= passwordField.getText(); 

 if (username.isEmpty() \|\| password.isEmpty()) { 

 System.out.println("Error: Fields cannot be empty.");  return; 

 } 

 System.out.println("Attempting login for: " \+ username);   

 *// In a real app, you would check the database here*  if (username.equals("admin") && password.equals("password123")) {  System.out.println("Login Successful\!"); 

 usernameField.setText(""); 

 passwordField.setText("");

Page **14** of **22**   
 } else { 

 System.out.println("Login Failed\!"); 

 } 

 } 

} 

**Step 4.2: Link the Button in Scene Builder** 

1\. Right-click login.fxml → **Open** (in Scene Builder). 2\. Select the **Login Button**. 

3\. In the Code panel (right side), look for **On Action**. 4\. Type: handleLoginButtonAction and press Enter. 5\. Save and close Scene Builder. 

**Step 4.3: Create the Main App Class** 

1\. Right-click programmaticdemo → **New → Java Class**. 2\. Name it FXMLApp. 

3\. Paste this code: 

java 

package programmaticdemo; 

import javafx.application.Application; 

import javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader; 

import javafx.scene.Parent; 

import javafx.scene.Scene; 

import javafx.stage.Stage; 

public class FXMLApp extends Application {

Page **15** of **22**   
 @Override 

 public void start(Stage primaryStage) throws Exception { 


 *// Load the FXML file* 

 FXMLLoader loader \= new FXMLLoader(getClass().getResource("login.fxml"));  Parent root \= loader.load(); 

 *// Create the scene* 

 Scene scene \= new Scene(root, 400, 350); 

 primaryStage.setTitle("JavaFX Login"); 

 primaryStage.setScene(scene); 

 primaryStage.show(); 

 } 

 public static void main(String\[\] args) { 

 launch(args); 

 } 

}
